source.title: Favorability of Loss Landscape with Regularization Requires Both Large Overparametrization and Initialization
source.authors: Etienne Boursier; Matthew Bowditch; Matthias Englert; Ranko Lazić

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and appendix. It is not cut off in the supplied excerpt, although it includes apparent typesetting/OCR artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes gradient-flow and gradient-descent outcomes in two-layer ReLU regression with ℓ2 regularization, testing initialization and width effects on convergence to global versus spurious solutions. This bears conceptually on the claim, but the task, loss, and models differ from benchmark classification.
record.gate_note: The paper’s results test initialization and overparametrization effects on regularized regression optimization. It does not test CIFAR classification, classification error, corrupted labels, depth, batch normalization, or learning-rate stability. Figure 1 reports cone proportions, not training outcomes; Figure 2 reports effective rank, not training error.
record.test_reason: The study reports related optimization results, but none tests a listed version. Its width experiments measure activation-cone geometry of regularized regression, rather than gradient-descent failure frequencies as teacher and student widths co-grow or the benefit of one or two extra neurons (V2). Its initialization experiments measure solution norm, rank and regularized optimality, rather than activation-matched signal propagation, training speed or trainable depth (V4).
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the main distinction between favorable landscape geometry and actual optimization. It needs a qualification: Theorem 2 proves convergence to suboptimal rank-one stationary networks under small balanced initialization, and Section 5 states that these are usually saddles because they contain zero neurons. Large width makes most activation cones favorable; orthogonal-data results show that exponential width can be necessary for global regularized optimality. Small-initialization solutions nevertheless retain simple, sparse representations.
record.recipe_differences: Two-layer ReLU regression with ℓ2-regularized square loss and gradient flow or gradient descent; the claim concerns benchmark classification and varied deep-network training recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scale changes the training dynamics and final solution: small scales favor sparse, rank-one spurious solutions, while larger scales can reach global minima in the reported synthetic regression experiments. Width changes the fraction of activation cones containing global minima and spurious local minima.

fits_no_version.finding: With width 100 and λ=10⁻⁵, synthetic regression experiments attain training MSE around 10⁻⁸ across initialization scales, while small scales yield higher norm and suboptimal regularized loss; larger scales approach the global optimum.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scale can determine regularized optimality despite near interpolation in two-layer ReLU regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Small initialization rapidly produces low-rank features, whereas large initialization retains full effective rank through interpolation and reduces rank much later.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scale controls the timing and structure of feature learning in the studied regularized regression problem.

fits_no_version.finding: Sampled activation cones increasingly contain global optima at large widths; these geometric proportions do not directly establish optimization success probabilities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large width favors activation-cone geometry for regularized two-layer ReLU regression.

fits_no_version.finding: For orthogonal inputs, Theorem 3 bounds the probability of non-global gradient-flow limit points below by 1−m2^(−n*), under its regularization and rotation-invariant initialization assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reaching globally optimal regularized solutions can require width exponential in the number of orthogonal training inputs, independently of initialization scale.

record.problems: The empirical experiments use synthetic regression data and two-layer networks, not benchmark classification. Figure 1 samples activation cones and does not directly measure optimization outcomes. Experimental results are reported over five runs/datasets, with min/max ranges but no formal confidence intervals. Theoretical statements apply under the paper’s stated assumptions.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. The paper’s theorems on convergence to spurious stationary points are described in the author-conclusion and fits_no_version fields; they do not measure any listed version’s classification-error outcome.

untested.parts: All: CIFAR classification error, convolutional networks, corrupted labels, and the stated training-recipe comparisons.

Gradient-descent spurious-local-minimum frequencies as teacher and student widths co-grow, and the effect of one or two additional student neurons within widths 6–20. V2 does not require classification; the mismatch concerns the objective, width comparison and measured outcome.
All depth, identity-shortcut, special-initialization and normalization-free residual comparisons.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, training-speed and trainable-depth comparisons, including orthogonal versus Gaussian weights.
All stability-threshold, curvature, sharpness, recovery and divergence results.
All batch-normalization and Fixup comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance.

record.verdict_notes: No listed version receives a verdict. The record incorrectly treats V2 as a classification claim and repeatedly treats classification error as a requirement shared by all versions. The theoretical results are declared in rows_left_out, so their absence as rows does not require a missing entry.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, SGD/Adam, and the stated model-size, early-stopping, and regularization comparisons.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student classification with spurious local minima frequencies as teacher/student widths co-grow and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Plain versus residual network depth comparisons on ImageNet or CIFAR-10, and the cited special-initialization or normalization-free residual conditions.
Activation-matched initialization effects on trainability, signal propagation, training speed, or trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization in very deep networks.
Learning-rate behavior above or below stability thresholds, loss/curvature trajectories, sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization versus no normalization comparisons of training speed, accuracy, or learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network (width m=100)
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on regularized square loss with initialization scale α swept across values.

conditions.value: d ∈ {3, 4, 5}; data generated as described in Appendix A.2.1

rows.measure: Final regularized loss minus optimal regularized loss
rows.value: Small initialization scales lead to convergence to a spurious local minimum; larger scales allow convergence toward the global minimum. Figure 9 reports the loss gap by initialization scale.
rows.uncertainty: Shaded areas show min/max deviations over 5 runs; no numerical values stated in text.
rows.locator: Appendix A.2, Figures 8–10; experimental details in Appendix A.2.1
rows.note: The text states the qualitative result and Figure 9 plots the gap; no exact plotted values are given. This is regularized regression rather than classification, so it is linked to no listed version.
rows.check: Figure 9 covers d ∈ {3,4,5}, not only d=5; its baseline is the global optimum computed by convex optimization. The stated α grid is explicit for the trajectory figures, and should not automatically be assigned to Figure 9. Appendix A.2 calls the small-scale endpoints local minima, but Section 5 explains that endpoints containing zero neurons are saddles. Describe them as suboptimal stationary solutions unless local minimality is established.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network (width m=100)
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on regularized square loss while varying initialization scale α.

conditions.value: α varied; values shown in Figure 8

rows.measure: Squared Euclidean norm of all weights after training
rows.baseline: A network only consisting of the teacher neuron has squared Euclidean norm 2.
rows.value: The final network size is markedly smaller for large α; as α decreases, it has a sharp transition and becomes close to 2.
rows.uncertainty: Min/max deviations over 5 runs are shown in Figure 8; no numerical values stated in text.
rows.note: This reports parameter norm, not the training-error behavior named by the claim versions.
rows.check: Parameter norm does not measure any listed version. The baseline of 2 is the teacher-only network's norm, not the globally optimal regularized network's norm.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network (width m=100)
rows.operation_detail: Track effective rank of the hidden weight matrix during training across initialization scales.
rows.measure: Effective rank of hidden weight matrix
rows.value: For large α, rank remains full for a long period after interpolation and falls during grokking; for small α, it rapidly decreases within fewer than 10³ epochs and remains low.
rows.uncertainty: Mean over 5 runs; shaded areas show min/max deviations.
rows.note: The result concerns feature rank and interpolation in regression, not classification error.
rows.check: Effective rank measures representation structure, not the speed or trainable depth named by V4.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU networks across sampled activation cones
rows.operation_detail: Sweep width and estimate the proportion of sampled nonempty activation cones whose closure contains a global minimum or which contain a spurious local minimum of regularized loss.

conditions.value: Independent Gaussian inputs; labels from a teacher two-layer ReLU network of width 10
5 random datasets; 100 sampled cones per procedure

rows.measure: Proportion of activation cones containing global minima or spurious local minima
rows.value: The proportion of cones containing global minima approaches 1 when width exceeds the number of nonempty neuron activation patterns; spurious-local-minimum proportion is close to 0 beyond that threshold and reaches a value of order 0.1 before it.
rows.uncertainty: Min/max deviations over 5 random datasets; 100 sampled cones.
rows.note: The study explicitly frames these as loss-landscape cone proportions, not observed training-error outcomes.
rows.check: These are sampled cone proportions, not optimization failure frequencies. Appendix A.1 operationalizes the orange series through a numerical stationarity check at a constrained minimizer; it does not independently establish unrestricted local minimality.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU networks across sampled activation cones
rows.operation_detail: Repeat the cone-proportion sweep, sampling cones from activation patterns of random Gaussian-initialized networks.

conditions.value: Independent Gaussian inputs; labels from a teacher two-layer ReLU network of width 10
Generate a random network with standard Gaussian weights and output scalars; observe its activation cone

rows.measure: Proportion of activation cones containing global minima or spurious local minima
rows.value: The observations are similar to Figure 1; the text says the result is relevant to typical neural network initializations.
rows.note: These are cone proportions, not training outcomes.
rows.check: Gaussian sampling weights activation cones by initialization probability, but no gradient-descent trajectories are measured. The numerical stationarity qualification for R4 also applies.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU networks on orthogonal datasets
rows.operation_detail: Sweep width and estimate proportions of activation cones containing global minima or local minima.

conditions.value: n random orthogonal unit vectors; labels from teacher two-layer ReLU network of width 10
Uniform over nonempty cones or random-network activation patterns; text says both are uniform in this setting

rows.measure: Proportion of activation cones containing global minima or spurious local minima
rows.value: The fraction with global minima rises around the activation-pattern width threshold; the fraction with spurious local minima is almost complementary, and is close to 1 for small m.
rows.note: This is a loss-landscape result; the text separately gives a theoretical gradient-flow claim, but it is not a classification-error measure.
rows.check: Figure 4 records cone geometry, not observed training outcomes. The separate gradient-flow theorem establishes non-global limit points under its assumptions, not necessarily convergence to local minima.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network (width m=100)
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on regularized square loss while varying initialization scale.
rows.measure: Mean square error on training data
rows.value: Mean square error in all experiments is in the region of 10⁻⁸; networks are approximate interpolators.
rows.note: The result is regression MSE under a specific synthetic setup, not classification error on a benchmark.
rows.check: The approximately 10⁻⁸ training MSE is a valid regression result, but does not measure V1's convolutional-network classification error on CIFAR.
